Females of Oligoneuriella rhenana emerge with a body length, excluding the caudal filaments, of 1.5 cm , while the slightly smaller males reach approximately 1.7 cm  at this final moult. The larval development of this rheophilic mayfly is prolonged, with emergence typically occurring 360 days after hatching  when the water temperature remains stable at 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This extended aquatic phase, spanning nearly a full year, is characteristic of univoltine populations inhabiting cool, well-oxygenated streams. The ultimate dry weight attained by mature nymphs just prior to metamorphosis has been measured at 2.0 mg , a value which reflects the accumulation of somatic tissues during the long larval period. Upon emergence, the teneral imago weighs approximately 0.0006 mg dry mass , a remarkably low initial weight that underscores the extreme investment in the subimaginal moult and the reliance on stored reserves for the short-lived adult stage.

Reproductive output in related heptageniid species, from which data for Oligoneuriella rhenana are partially drawn, provides a useful comparative framework. The cumulative number of eggs produced by a single female, recorded under controlled laboratory conditions at 16 °C [T = 16 °C], amounts to 2500 eggs . This fecundity estimate, originally documented for Ecdyonurus dispar, is considered representative for O. rhenana given their similar body size and life-history strategy. The vast majority of these eggs are deposited during a single oviposition event shortly after the imago moult, a pattern consistent with the semelparous reproductive mode common among mayflies. At the prevailing temperature of 16 °C, embryonic development proceeds rapidly, though the precise thermal requirements for optimal hatching success remain an active area of investigation for this species in its native Central European streams.

The embryonic incubation period, again drawing on data from Ecdyonurus dispar as a reliable proxy, lasts 25 days [ab = 25 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Prolonged incubation at lower thermal regimes would presumably extend this duration, a common pattern across ephemeropteran development. The larval phase that follows is the dominant period of biomass accumulation and morphological growth, culminating in the final instar nymph that will eventually undergo metamorphosis. The initial dry weight of the newly hatched larva, computed from the egg mass and fecundity, is 0.0006 mg , a figure that represents the minute starting capital for the feeding larva. This value aligns closely with what would be expected for a yolk-dependent embryo transitioning to exogenous feeding on periphytic algae and detritus in the interstitial spaces of gravel-bed streams.

Once the imago emerges, its lifespan as a winged adult is remarkably brief, lasting only 7 days [am = 7 days] at an ambient temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This ephemeral adult stage is dedicated almost exclusively to reproduction; the imago does not feed, and its remaining energy reserves are rapidly depleted during swarming and mating. Comparing this to the far longer juvenile period of nearly one year, the contrast is striking and defines the species as a classic example of a 'capital breeder' that invests all acquired resources into a single, synchronized reproductive bout. The adult male, with its body length of 1.7 cm , is slightly smaller than the female but compensates with a more streamlined form suited to aerial pursuit during the mating dance over the stream surface. The 2.0 mg  of dry mass accumulated by the larva provides the entire energetic budget for this final, critical life phase.

The relationship between the initial egg mass and the final larval body size highlights the efficiency of nutrient acquisition during the 360-day instar period (360 days)  at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. At the cool stream temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C] typical of its habitat, the slow developmental rate permits a gradual but steady assimilation of organic matter. The 1.5 cm  female body length represents a typical size threshold for reproductive maturity in this species, sufficient to accommodate the 2500 eggs  produced at a temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. Under the warmer conditions of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] that characterize the adult flight season, the imago must complete its reproductive mission within its 7-day lifespan (7 days) [am = 7 days]. The initial dry weight of the hatching larva, 0.0006 mg , is three orders of magnitude smaller than the ultimate dry weight of the mature nymph, a growth trajectory that underscores the profound developmental plasticity of life in a seasonally predictable, resource-rich lotic environment.
